speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon, J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, while under ordinary circumstances no mention is made of those who are in the gallery, because according to tradition there are none who occupy positions other than on the floor of the house, I think hon. members will permit me to refer to the fact that there are in the gallery today two outstanding representatives of the United States of America, members of the cabinet of President Kennedy. I refer to Hon. Orville Freeman, secretary of agriculture, and Hon. Stewart Udall, secretary of the interior.
They are here in pursuance of the course being followed by our two nations whereby there is the widest possible consultation between members of the government of Canada and members of the administration of the United States. They are here to meet their opposite numbers, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and one or two other ministers. I am sure the house will join with me in a warm welcome to them, and at the same time we wish to convey through them to the President that we are looking forward with anticipation to the visit of the President of the United States and Mrs. Kennedy next week.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MEMBERS OF U.S. CABINET
speechtext: It gives me a great deal of pleasure, on behalf of our party, to associate myself and my friends with the welcome that has been expressed to our distinguished visitors by the Prime Minister. They are, indeed, very welcome and I only hope they feel as much at home in Ottawa as we always do when we go to Washington.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MEMBERS OF U.S. CABINET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this group wishes to associate itself with the welcoming and kind remarks expressed by the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition. We trust that these gentlemen will enjoy their stay in Ottawa and learn a great deal.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the house is in a little more amiable mood this afternoon. This motion stands in the name of the chairman of the standing committee on standing orders. I am the vice chairman of that committee. I wish, on behalf of the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), to move:
That the tenth report of the standing committee on standing orders, presented to the house on Thursday, May 4, 1961, be now concurred in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not rising to withhold consent but to raise a point of order with respect to the motion itself. Your Honour will recall that the hon. member for Essex East attempted to move a motion on Tuesday, May 2, as a private member of this house, and Your Honour made an extended ruling at that time, the effect of which was that these motions that appear on routine proceedings affecting the business of the house can be moved only by the house leader. You pointed out specifically to the hon. member, as reported on page 4210 of Hansard:
The hon. member raises the question of whether a private member can do the same thing.
In other words, he raised the question of whether or not a private member could move a motion with respect to the business of the house. Your Honour went on to say:
I think it is clear that a private member can do so if he can use the notice of motion procedure which is open to private members under our rules.
Your Honour then went on to point out that this would be, at this stage of the session, a completely ineffective procedure because the notices of motion are not even printed. It does seem that so far as the house is concerned, the hon. lady, whatever she may be in the committee, is a private member of the house; yet her notice of motion is printed under "Motions" in the routine proceedings. The point I am raising is whether it is open to one hon. member who is not the leader of the house to move a motion with respect to the business of the house, and not open to another hon. member to do so.

May I refer to the report of proceedings for February 5, 1954, when Mr. Harrison, who was chairman of the standing orders committee, presented the first report of that committee. He filed a notice of motion in his name for concurrence in that report on February 8, 1954. On February 8, 1954, Mr. Carter, for Mr. Harrison, moved concurrence in that report. This was not done by leave of the house.
In 1955 Mr. Harrison, having presented the first report of the standing orders committee on April 1, 1955, gave notice of motion for concurrence on April 4. However, on April 4 Mr. Hanna, for Mr. Harrison, moved concurrence in the report. Again Mr. Harrison, having presented the second report of the standing orders committee on May 28, 1956, and notice having been given for concurrence therein, Mr. Fairey, for Mr. Harrison, moved concurrence on June 8.
Coming to the present session or this present parliament-

speechtext: This is not the point at issue, Mr. Speaker.

The consent of the house was not asked nor was it required on that occasion. Again on March 27-

speechtext: Order. I think I might save the house some time by saying to the hon. member that I think it is clear that the motion for concurrence in the report of a committee has for a good many years customarily been moved in the house by the chairman of the committee. Whether that procedure is in accordance with the rules of the house or is a practice that has grown up in contravention of the rules is really the point at issue, I think. However, before dealing with that matter, may I ask whether I am correct in assuming that the house will permit the hon.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Just on that point, Your Honour, may I say this. As I understood the point raised by the hon. member, it was that these motions should be made by the leader of the house. Am I not correct in that respect?

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
All I can say, and I think all that need be said, in answer to that point, Your Honour, is that I have already given many illustrations where motions of this kind were not made by the leader of the house; nor has is it ever been the practice or the usage, as far as my research has indicated, that any such motion has ever been required to be made by the leader of the house.
May I say this also. If that were the requirement, then by analogy, motions dealing with late petitions which are to be referred to the standing committee on standing orders would normally then be made by the leader of the house. Yet the practice has been and is that they have not been made by him.
I can give many instances. Here is a motion made on April 21, 1955, with regard to West-coast Transmission Company Limited, which was sponsored by Mr. Fairey. On this occasion Mr. Hunter moved that the late petition be referred to the standing committee on standing orders.
Again, on February 13, 1953, the sponsor of that motion was Mr. Macnaughton, who moved that the late petition be referred to the standing orders committee. In that case it was done by leave of the house, but in any event it was not done by the leader of the government.
On March 2, 1954, Mr. Hunter, who was not chairman of the standing orders committee but was chairman of another committee, moved for another sponsor, Mr. Balcolm, that a late petition relating to the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company be referred to the standing committee on standing orders.
Then we had the same thing happen in this house not very long ago. I cannot give the date, but the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) moved the reference of late petitions with which the standing orders committee dealt. These petitions are dealt with in this report. The motion referring

those petitions to the standing committee on standing orders was made as stated by the hon. member for Davenport and not by the leader of the house.
As you said the other day, sir, when I believe a motion was being made by the whip, a practice and usage that has been well established in this house should not be interfered with or changed without the strongest authority. Here are authorities from 1953 up to the present time where none of those motions was made by the house leader.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we are all indebted to my hon. friend from Essex West for the precedents he has laid down. It seems to me that all the arguments he has advanced in favour of the course that he proposes in respect of a motion moved by one private member would apply with equal validity to the motion proposed by my hon. friend from Essex East, I think on May 2.
With great respect, the point of order raised by my hon. friend for Bonavista-Twillingate does not deal with that matter at all. Perhaps it might save time if this motion were allowed to stand so that you would have time to consider the very important point of order raised by my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Essex West whether there is any urgency to have this report reviewed?

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I speak to the question of urgency. We have standing on the order paper a bill respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway for the construction of a line which will provide employment not only in the construction of the railway but also in the plant or industry this railway is intended to serve. Unless this report is concurred in that legislation now standing on the order paper, which has already been passed by the other place, cannot be dealt with in this house.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out, on the question of urgency, that it cannot be dealt with by this house until a week from tomorrow in any event.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say further, apropos the point made by the Leader of the Opposition, that I do not think the two motions are in any way analogous. The motion made by the hon. member for Essex East was an oral motion.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was later put in writing.

maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It was not a motion made on notice. The point in issue there was whether
Standing Orders Committee or not it was within the power or privileges of an ordinary hon. member for the house- which of course hon. members sitting on the other side now are, in as much as they no longer occupy the treasury benches-to make such a motion orally. That was the point, and the only point, in issue. Any comments or observations Your Honour may have made must be interpreted in terms of the fact that the hon. member was attempting to make a motion, founded on oral notice of motion. If the proper procedure had been followed, it would be coming before the house under the order of notices of motions in the names of private members. That is not what this is; it is a motion on routine proceedings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STANDING ORDERS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO MOVE CONCURRENCE IN TENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think since the question of the propriety of our practice has been raised it might be well if some consideration were given to it. However, we have followed the practice which has been used today for a good many years, and I should not like to interrupt a procedure which is well established without having clear authority to do so. It may be that we have developed a practice which is contrary to the rules, so what I propose to do is to accept the motion as it has been moved, without prejudice to the point being raised again, and I will give consideration myself to whether the house has departed from the rules in accepting a motion of this kind from a private member.
I have no difficulty in distinguishing this motion from the one which was made by the hon. member for Essex East, because there the question was whether his motion could come under routine proceedings. I was disposed to think that was a handicap, an obstacle, which the hon. member had not overcome, in addition to the question of lack of notice and the other question of whether the leader of the house should move such a motion. So I do distinguish the motion which has been referred to from this motion, which can clearly be made under routine proceedings and which has been made after notice. The only question is whether the leader of the house should undertake this responsibility.
I can cite one other instance where the leader of the house does not perform this responsibility. Formal and routine motions to change the personnel of standing committees have regularly been moved in the house by a private member rising and moving that certain names be substituted for others, and the house has accepted that procedure. However, I do not wish to determine the issue finally at this time, and if hon. members wish

Business o} the House to raise the matter further I shall be receptive to argument about it. But in the circumstances I will put the motion which has been moved by the hon. member for Essex West.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speechtext: This motion would not have been necessary had the government been aware of the rules of the house and had the government not been asleep, as it has accused others of being, several days ago. This motion should have been moved long before Saturday-

speechtext: Order. Before the hon. member for Laurier proceeds on that line may I say that I do not think it is relevant to fight over again the battles of Saturday on this motion. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speechtext:
I should first like to read the motion. It says:
That on Saturday, May 13, 1961, and every Saturday thereafter until the end of the session the order of business and procedure shall be as for Thursday, a government day.
I submit, with deference, that I have the right to deal with matters that are mentioned in that motion. Any attempt to infringe the right which I claim I have to deal with the matters which are contained therein would be, I submit, an invasion of the rights of a member of parliament.
I would say at the beginning that the necessity for this motion being placed on the order paper arose out of a defect in the amendment which was passed on April 24. When the house decided at that time to hold Saturday sittings, a motion such as this should have been passed. The house then decided to sit on Saturday, but no provision was made in that order for the business to be dealt with on that day. That defect could have been corrected by the government, and only by the government. However, until today and, of course, Friday, no action was taken by the government in this respect. Your Honour's


ruling of May 2 is ample proof of my statement. Therefore I say the neglect of the government resulted in the fiasco which took place on Saturday. We were faced with a blank order paper.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: ORDER OF BUSINESS FOR SATURDAY SITTINGS

The other comments which the hon. member is making seem to me to be relevant enough, but to my mind it would not be relevant to deal at length with the events of Saturday morning because this motion does not have any bearing on that particular situation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

In order to avoid putting the house in an absurd position Your Honour was obliged to rescue the government, to rescue the situation-

We heard 12 speakers on one of the items on the order paper. All those speeches added absolutely nothing either by way of material or in any other way to the proceedings of the house. maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

Business of the House
on this occasion to discuss the antecedents of this motion, including the Prime Minister's statement on April 24, when he explained to the house that we should sit on Saturday to discuss, as he said then, matters which would not arouse controversy, noncontroversial matters. I should like to deal specifically, Mr. Speaker, with the question of the order of business to be followed next Saturday and on subsequent Saturdays. The motion says that it shall be as for Thursday. Now, the house leader and, on one occasion, the Minister of National Revenue, made some rather impassioned comments concerning the rights of private members and the private members' hour. They said there were many hon. members who had notices of motions and bills on the order paper, and those members were entitled to deal with those matters. I draw your attention to the fact that there are some 67 items under public bills and orders, which include public bills in the hands of private members.
While public bills in the hands of private members are not allowed to come to a vote because of the embarrassing circumstances that develop therefrom, nevertheless, as I am sure members of the government would agree, the discussion on these bills affords private members an opportunity of expressing opinions on specific subject matters. Undoubtedly the government is influenced by these expressions of opinion and, undoubtedly, in subsequent years legislation is introduced covering these subjects. In this way a private member, whether he be on the government side or the opposition side, has an opportunity of expressing his point of view and eventually seeing

Division
that point of view come to fruition in legislative form. We have had a number of experiences of this kind.
When it was proposed to sit on Saturday, I think practically every member in the house was in agreement that we should have Saturday sittings. In fact, it was the hon. member for Port Arthur who moved that motion, and I seconded it. We did not hear too much objection from members, other than those who occupy the front benches to my left. Theirs was a sort of weak objection after the event. In view of the contribution that private members can make by discussing public bills, and as a sort of recognition by the government of the fact that the majority of members in this house were agreeable to sitting on Saturday, I move:
That the motion he amended by deleting the word "Thursday" and substituting therefor the word "Friday".
In this way some of the rights and opportunities of private members in this house could be properly recognized.

Right	Hon.	J.	G.	Diefenbaker	(Prime

On May 3 the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed the house that the commission had agreed on a report to the cochairmen and was now ready to proceed to Laos to undertake its tasks of verification and supervision. I am informed that the commission left New Delhi yesterday en route to Laos, and is expected to arrive shortly. Eleven officers, six non-commissioned officers and two communications technicians from Canada have left for Asia. Additional Canadian military and civilian personnel required in connection with the commission's task will be available if necessary. Those to whom I have referred left Vancouver last night by air on their way to Saigon.
Incidentally, the government has received no intimation that there have been any serious violations of the de facto cease fire which has existed in Laos since Thursday, May 4.

This parade had been ordered, and a decision had to be made by 7.30 in the morning whether to go ahead with it or not. speakerposition: topic
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the early days of the present session, and particularly in the period prior

to the Christmas recess, this government sought to introduce and succeeded in introducing a series of legislative measures which were mentioned in the speech from the throne, and which were directed primarily toward relieving the complex problems which the country is facing in this period of uncertainty and confusion.
The official opposition co-operated fully with the government and went so far as to waive the debate on the speech from the throne in order to enable the house to receive and discuss the government's proposals with a minimum of delay. The co-operation of the opposition was such that the specific proposals introduced by the government to deal with unemployment and the other economic problems were passed with a minimum of discussion. The co-operation was such that on the last sitting day before the adjournment for the Christmas recess, the house leader was in a position to state that the house, in the short period of 25 sitting days, had already dealt with five pieces of legislation, as well as the budget. The nature of this budget is well known to the country, and it has been said that it raised more questions than it answered.
Today, Mr. Speaker, is the 100th sitting day of the present session. One would be inclined to believe that in that period of close to six months, in 100 full sitting days, the government would have been in a position to introduce a piece of legislation which would have been directed toward correcting one of the best examples of maladministration and mismanagement by the government of the day. I realize that some of the members of the government are showing signs of anxiety, signs of uneasiness, which I can well understand, because at this very moment they are asking themselves, what amendment will the opposition present to this supply motion?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, some hon. gentlemen opposite are laughing. Perhaps they are relieved. The subject of the amendment to the supply motion is one of grave concern to the entire population of our country. In this period of unprecedented indecision we have a government which has accepted the principle of responsibility, a government whose Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he sat on the opposition side showed such ardour for responsible government but who now rejects some of the responsibility which he so earnestly attributed to his predecessor. In the course of the present session, we have had numerous illustrations of the Minister
Unemployment Insurance of Finance shrinking away from his responsibility and from his part in responsible government. This is the same hon. member who, only five years ago, gave this house such impassioned lectures on the principles of responsible government, but who is now rejecting categorically any suggestions that he has responsibility for certain policies. He insists that he has no role in the matter at all.
The amendment which I intend to introduce at the conclusion of my remarks will concern not only the Minister of Finance but also another member of the government who, I notice, seems very anxious to be relieved of the anxiety facing him at the moment. I want to state now the subject which I intend to develop in more detail in initiating the debate on the amendment to this supply motion.
The employers and employees of this country are up in arms. They are not satisfied with the present administration's application of the Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations. The rapid and continuous depletion of the unemployment insurance fund is-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The minister is always rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: With very good reason, too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Yes, the minister is always interrupting members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Here is the pot
calling the kettle black, the terrible tempered Mr. Bang from Laurier.
The hon. member who has the floor began by raising as a grievance, apparently, something in relation to the question of responsible government and whatever part the Minister of Finance was thought to have played in that issue. Now he is going on to a second question. It is a rule of this house, Mr. Speaker, that before any member, in such a debate, may pass on to a second grievance all hon. members who wish to be heard on the first grievance are entitled to be heard. The hon. member having chosen to raise this question as a grievance, I claim my right as a member of this house to speak in reply to it. The hon. member is choosing now to run away from that grievance and raise a second question. This has been typical of the tactics of the opposition in these supply motions during the present session.
On the last two supply motions, Mr. Speaker, which were on March 20 and April 24, you had occasion to make a ruling under just such circumstances to try to curb the excesses of the opposition and the way in

Unemployment Insurance which they are seeking to ride roughshod over the rules of this house. The rights of other hon. members are at stake. The hon. member who has the floor on such a motion is not the only member who has rights in such a situation. He having chosen to make an attack in relation to this question of responsible government, and the relationship of at least one member of the government to that issue, I claim the right to discuss that subject before another grievance is raised in the house by anyone.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
With all due respect to the Minister of Finance, may I say it is true that the hon. member who was initiating a grievance used at first what has been fittingly described in the past as a scattergun. I do not think he came down definitely enough in his aim on any particular subject to say that he was introducing a grievance. It is true that he did connect the Minister of Finance with some issue of responsible government, but what issue I was not able to determine.
As I understood him, he now has raised as a grievance the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance sticks his neck out on these subjects.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I thought I made it clear in my remarks that the amendment which I intended to introduce this afternoon had something to do with the responsibility of the Minister of Finance and the responsibility of another member of government. The amendment has to do with the application of the Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations.
As I have said, the rapid and continuous depletion of the employment insurance fund is one of the most urgent problems which this government is called upon to face in this session. We understand this problem will require an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The policies of the present government since taking office, and the actions of the government, have resulted in practically wiping out a fund over $920 million built up under a Liberal administration. The unemployment insurance fund, we all know, consists of moneys contributed by the employees, by the employers and by the government. These moneys are held in trust by the government and used for the payment of benefits to the unemployed.
When the act was introduced in 1940 by a Liberal government, it was introduced as an act to establish an unemployment insurance commission, to provide for insurance against unemployment, to establish an employment


service, and for other purposes related thereto. Since its introduction in 1940 this act has been amended on various occasions such as in 1955, 1956, 1957 and more recently, 1959. Notwithstanding the amendments to the act or to these regulations the principle remained the same. It consisted of a fund contributed by employers, employees and the government for the payment of benefits to the unemployed. When the act was introduced in 1940, the mover of the resolution had this to say. As reported at page 1650 of Hansard of July 16, 1940, these are the words of Mr. McLarty, the then minister of labour:
This done, it will be recorded of the present generation that at a time when we were bending every effort and endeavour to overcoming the enemy at our gate we were not unconscious of our duty and our obligation to promote the welfare and happiness of our own people.
On July 19, speaking on the second reading of this bill, the then hon. member for Essex East as reported at page 1779 of Hansard of that year, had this to say about this bill:
I conclude by saying to the Minister of Labour, coming as he does and as I do from an area in which there is unemployment for many months of the year because of the type of industry that predominates in the community, he will have done nothing in his public life greater than to create this measure when he is able to say at the conclusion of this session, as I hope he will be able to say, to his people and to all the people throughout the country that one further great reform for a harassed group of our population has finally been realized.
It was realized, Mr. Speaker, again by a Liberal government.
In 1959, the present government saw fit to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. As a result of the amendments introduced at that time the employees were estimated to derive additional benefits amounting to approximately $20 million per year. At the same time contributions by both employers and employees were increased by approximately 30 per cent. By such a move employers and employees were called upon to contribute yearly an additional $80 million or $90 million while the government's contribution remained at the same level or proportion. As a result of lack of policy by the present government that fund which was built up to $900 million under a Liberal government was being almost completely wiped out in less than four years of Conservative administration.
In addressing this house on April 4 of last year, I warned the government that, at the present rate of Canada's unemployment, the unemployment insurance fund would be just about wiped out by March 31, 1962. Mr. Speaker, I was a good conservative in my estimate at that time. I was accused at the time of being a prophet of doom and gloom. However, the fact remains that a fund which

had been depleted by almost $600 million since the present government took office in 1957 up to April of 1960, has now, a year later, reached an additional sum of $140 million, and to this will be added a further deficit of approximately $40 million when the figures for the month of April are made public. At the present rate the balance in the fund will be in the vicinity of $95 million to $100 million at the end of May and it will be even lower on the last day of June of this year.
While this fund has been going down over the last four years-and we must admit that it will be practically wiped out by this time next year-what action has the government been taking to safeguard this fund which was designed to be stable and self-perpetuating? Sessional paper No. 83 which was tabled on December 21, 1960, the very day on which the house took recess for the Christmas season, reports on the conclusions arrived at by the unemployment insurance advisory committee resulting from their meeting of October 27, 1960. I quote the conclusions arrived at as found at page 6 of sessional paper No. 83, tabled in this house on Wednesday, December 21, 1960:
As hereinbefore stated the fund will probably be reduced at March 31, 1961, to under $150 million and by the end of the seasonal benefit payments, say at May 31st, 1961, will be not more than $85 million.
The committee finds no grounds upon which to modify the recommendations contained in its reports of July 8, 1958, and July 27, 1960 and respectfully and urgently repeats its previous recommendations regarding increasing the government's contribution and also replenishing the fund by a grant as recommended in the July, 1960 report. The committee expressed confidence that the government will take suitable action.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, five months have passed since the government was handed this recommendation and as yet no action has been taken. The government has failed to justify the confidence expressed by members of the advisory committee. What are the main reasons for this constant depletion of the fund which had proved to be so secure and so sound under the previous Liberal administration? I know that some will try to blame the inclusion or the admission of fishermen under the unemployment insurance benefits. May I say that this is not the reason; this is not the case. I want to remind those who are blaming the fishermen for the depletion of the fund that they had better revise their conclusions. In fact, the unemployment insurance advisory committee itself in its report referred to earlier, suggested that the loss to the fund by extending benefits to fishermen should be paid from sources other than regular contributions.
Unemployment Insurance
I will not undertake at this time to review or refute the recommendation made by the advisory committee so far as benefits to fishermen are concerned. However, what I want to make clear is the fact that a fisherman well earns and well deserves his unemployment insurance benefits. The majority of our fishermen on the east coast, with the exception of those in some sections of Nova Scotia and those in very few areas of Newfoundland, are engaged in fishing for a period of six months to seven months per year. During that period the majority of them work from 18 hours to 20 hours per day, and in most cases six days a week. When, as happens in my own constituency of Gloucester, the dragger fishermen leave the wharf after midnight on Sunday and do not return before the following Friday or Saturday, and when during this period their diesel motors have been running for 24 hours a day, when winter comes or when the month of November or December is reached, these men deserve to return to their families and draw their unemployment insurance benefits during the winter months. I challenge any hon. member of this house to get up and deny the right of these brave men to share in the scheme of this insurance against unemployment. When the season of storms is raging, when heavy sheets of ice are covering our harbours and inlets we cannot expect these men to remain at their usual occupations or to carry on with their fishing operations.
At this very late date, May 8, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean), rose in this house and announced a further delay in the opening date of the lobster season. Why? For the very reason which I have just mentioned, because when here in Ottawa tulips are blooming in front of the parliament buildings, our fishermen of northern New Brunswick, of some sections of Prince Bdward Island and the Gaspe coast are waiting anxiously for the ice to move out before they can go to sea and set their fishing gear. Those men deserve to share in the unemployment insurance benefits, and they cannot be blamed for the depletion of the fund which has taken place in the last four years.
It is true-and the reports of the advisory committee make reference to it-that they have contributed to the maximum amount of $10 million in a full year in draining the unemployment insurance fund. In fact in the first three years when the fishermen were drawing benefits, they contributed approximately $23 million to the fund's loss. If other means have to be found to finance the fishermen's share of the benefits, it is the duty of the government to come up with a satisfactory solution.

Unemployment Insurance
Neither am I prepared to accept the interpretation which the unemployment insurance commission today is imposing on certain fishermen with regard to contributions and benefits, particularly for the year 1959. I know of certain fishermen who have contributed to unemployment insurance stamps for the period they were engaged in fishing operations during the summer and fall of 1959. At the close of the season, in October or November, the fish buyer purchased the necessary stamps to be used in payment of contributions, in accordance with instructions received from officials of the commission. The insurance stamps were affixed in the fisherman's unemployment insurance book by the dealer, as the employer of the fisherman, or the buyer of his fish, on the basis of the gross value of his landings less the required 25 per cent to be deducted for expenses.
I know of instances where a number of fishermen were awarded certain benefits during the winter of 1960 based on their earnings during the fishing season of 1959, and only a few months ago, during the winter months of 1961 they were forced to pay back 50 per cent or more of the benefits they had received during the previous winter months.
If a fisherman is idle during the winter months it is because he cannot carry on his fishing operations, because he is prevented from doing so by ice conditions or other factors beyond his control.
The gallantry and courage of our fishermen must be recognized by every hon. member of this house. I am sure that none of us has forgotten the tragedy of the Eseuminac fishermen in June, 1959, or the loss of a number of lives off the southern Nova Scotia coast only a month or so ago.
In fact, on this very day at 9 p.m. an investiture will take place in Fredericton by His Excellency the Governor General for the Eseuminac fishermen. These fishermen will receive the British Empire medal for gallantry and bravery shown toward their fellow fishermen during the storm of June, 1959.
This is why I ask the question at this time, who is responsible for the depletion of the unemployment insurance fund, if not the present government? Who is responsible for a loss of close to $28 million from October, 1958 to September, 1960, a period of two years?
The unemployment insurance fund account consists of the funds contributed by employees, employers and the government. This fund is held in trust and used for the payment of benefits to the unemployed. The governing statute provides that these funds shall be invested in government of Canada direct or guaranteed securities only.

Who is responsible for the investments of the unemployment insurance fund, if not the governor of the Bank of Canada together with two other representatives appointed, one by the Minister of Finance and the other by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr)? The facts are that by the end of March, 1958-

This fund was being managed not for the welfare and security of its beneficiaries, the unemployed of this country, the workers of this country, but to facilitate government debt management operations.

As a result of such transactions, as a result of this mismanagement for which the government must share the responsibility, the unemployment insurance fund, from the time this government took office, has been deprived of close to $70 million, three times as much as was lost through payment of benefits to fishermen.
The Minister of Finance cannot deny this. In the report-

-tabled on December 21 last we find a table showing month by month the losses to the fund from the sale of securities. I will not put all those figures on the record; there are too many. I mention in particular, however, that in some months losses have reached millions of dollars. I quote from this table, "Unemployment insurance fund selected figures taken from commission's monthly report", to illustrate my point. In 1958, in the month of November, $1,597,000 lost; in December, $3,169,000 lost; in February, 1959, $2,230,000; in March, $4,526,000. Later on, in 1959, in the month of December, $1,465,000. In 1960, in February, $3,209,000; in March, $2,825,000; June, $3,631,000; August, $1,393,000. And so on. The total losses exceed $28 million.
Surely, even if the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his colleagues brag about the magnitude of the drain on the fund this does not justify the government in showing a reckless disregard for the resting trust laid upon it to protect the integrity of a fund which is the property of the employers and of the workers of this country.
It may be of some interest to members of this house and to the country to note while the fund is being continuously depleted, its revenues are increasing at the rate of $7 million to $8 million a month. In fact, for the 12 months ending September 30, 1960, revenues were $94 million above the previous year.
I have mentioned two causes which have contributed to some extent to the depletion of the unemployment insurance fund. These, totalling an amount in the vicinity of $100 million, represent but a minor portion of the fantastic reduction of over $700 million in less than four years. The main factor contributing to this depletion is, by far, the ever increasing number of unemployed which factor is responsible for this great drain and for this heavy load of payments during the last four years.
I cannot understand a party or a government which takes pride in increasing unemployment insurance benefits from $231 million to $415 million in one single year. This is, 90205-6-285
Unemployment Insurance however, exactly what the present government is doing today in its pamphlet listing the records and accomplishment of the present administration.
The purpose of this fund is to pay benefits to an insured person when a specified contingency occurs. No insurance fund, no insurance of any kind, can exist under such a pressure as has been exerted on the unemployment insurance fund during the last four years. The plight of the unemployment insurance fund is a serious reminder that a country with 18 million people cannot afford to have three quarters of a million or more of its workers idle, producing nothing and acting only as a drain on the whole economy of the country. The man who draws unemployment insurance benefits of $25 or $30 a week is contributing very little to the gross national product of the country.
Year in and year out, unemployment may have become part of our Canadian way of life, but at no time in our history has it reached the high rate which is becoming an inevitable and established fact under a Conservative administration. How can a fund subsist with
869.000 claimants in February 1958, with
795.000 in the same month of 1959, with
823.000	in March of 1960 and 837,000 in March of this year?
Those same hundreds of thousands of claimants for unemployment insurance benefits are men without work and men seeking work. With very few exceptions, those same men or women would rather earn their living and that of their families by working by the sweat of their brows than remain idle at home with a mere $25 or $30 a week as their only source of revenue.
I agree, and I am the first one to admit, that there have been abuses, that there have been cases of fraud in connection with unemployment insurance benefits. It is the duty of the commission to take necessary steps to prevent such abuses and to take action against those who have been illegally receiving payments for unearned contributions. This does not mean, however, that qualified workers, men who for years have been accepted for benefits, should all at once be disqualified in order to salvage the perilous rate of the unemployment insurance fund.
Why should carpenters, painters and other types of workers be, all at once, automatically disqualified and deprived of benefits formerly awarded to them under similar conditions, as was done in February and March of this year. Why must a carpenter hired for a period of 14 to 18 weeks, to build a new home at a fixed rate of $10 or $12 a day, be deprived of his benefits if he becomes idle for a certain period during the winter months?

Unemployment Insurance
I know the minister will come back and tell the house that the unemployment insurance commission had no alternative in such cases. The minister will tell us that such decisions were reached following a ruling of the umpire appointed under provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act as the final authority for deciding on questions of insurability, and that the commission is obliged to follow his interpretation.
I will ask the minister why has it taken the commission 20 years to obtain a new ruling on section 27 (p) of the act which reads as follows:
-employment of a casual nature otherwise than for the purpose of the employer's trade or business;
Why should a widow who wants to have a new house built or her old house repaired or painted be denied the right to purchase unemployment insurance stamps for her employees? Why should a veteran who contracts to have a new home built under the Veterans' Land Act be prevented from giving his employees unemployment insurance stamps when he himself supervises the construction?
The widow in question needs a home to provide shelter for herself and her children, and her main interest or business is to remain in that home to look after her children. The veteran, whether employed as a civil servant or as a clerk, is not interested in hiring employees for his business or trade, but he is keenly interested in providing his wife and family with a new home.
Hundreds of cases have been brought to my attention in the last few months in which carpenters, labourers, and others have been deprived of their unemployment insurance benefits on the ground that they had been engaged in employment of a casual nature otherwise than for the purpose of the employer's trade or business. I ask again, why did it take the commission 20 years to arrive at such an arbitrary interpretation of the act?
The same employees who are being deprived for their benefits are being told, "Oh, yes, you can qualify for benefits if you are engaged as a carpenter or a painter, but what you have to do is to work for a building contractor who is licensed with the unemployment insurance commission and who is qualified to purchase stamps".
Is the minister aware of the effect of such a decision in rural areas where in many instances building contractors do not even exist? This means that an individual who wants to repair his house or build a new one must approach an outside contractor to do the job; that is, if he wants his workers to qualify for benefits. In many instances, this contractor will come in with his own men who also will

be outsiders. I ask the minister, is this the kind of fair play promised by the Prime Minister in his bill of rights?
This house has been sitting for over five months, and the minister has known of this new interpretation of the act for some time. If there was no alternative, what has prevented the minister from introducing an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act which would have resulted in justice for thousands of workers who are now being deprived of benefits for which they normally would have qualified for a number of years? What did the minister do? Instead of taking action to protect the claimants involved, instead of taking action to prevent such injustice, orders were issued on March 27 to every post office in the country to return immediately form 419C, known as "Application to purchase unemployment insurance stamps as a casual employer".
The Minister of Labour was aware of what was going on, and notwithstanding the fact this house has been sitting for the last five months, we are still waiting for the amendment to the act promised in the speech from the throne. We on this side of the house have been warning the Minister of Labour and the government as to the necessity and urgency of replenishing the unemployment insurance fund. We have also warned the minister that if he hopes to use the same method he used in 1959 he will meet with serious objections from this side of the house, and he will no doubt incur the wrath of Canadian employers and employees.
Instead of acting at once, instead of taking the necessary steps to protect the rights of thousands of workers, the minister and the government have preferred to see this large number of claimants who were being denied unemployment insurance benefits seek new assistance under the social assistance act. In doing this the government had the assurance that 50 per cent of the cost of such assistance had to be borne by the provinces and the municipalities.
If the Prime Minister, as he stated in Prince Albert on February 14, 1958, had succeeded "in defeating the problem of unemployment" the perilous position of the unemployment insurance fund would not exist today. We remember that in Brantford on February 17, 1958, he said that "the humblest of our people will not be forgotten. The people who are unemployed will not be put in the false position of being put on relief". Well, this is actually what is happening today with the new interpretation of the Unemployment Insurance Act under which claimants are being denied unemployment insurance benefits which they have earned. They have had to go and beg for social assistance, 50 per cent
[Mr. Robichaud.l

of which is paid by the provinces and the municipalities. Nobody has forgotten these words of the Prime Minister on a live telecast on February 18, 1958, when he said:
As long as I am Prime Minister of this country I am not going to blame anyone for unemployment.
Again, on February 24 of the same year he said at Cornwall:
We have acted. We are meeting unemployment. We have given young Canadians the hope. We have given them the vision.
The vision of the Prime Minister is very deceptive to the young and old of this country after four years of Conservative administration. It is very deceptive to the three quarters of a million unemployed who are depending on unemployment insurance benefits. For those workers who are without work the vision of 1958 has proved to exist only in the imagination of the Prime Minister.

The fact remains that the main reason for the present situation of the unemployment insurance fund is the large number of claimants, which figure has increased by at least 75 per cent to 80 per cent since the present government took office. In other words, if the present government had listened to the constructive suggestions made in this house by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and other opposition members, such a situation would not exist today.
The unemployment insurance fund is being depleted; it is being wiped out at an alarming rate and this government sits idle, refusing to take adequate measures to bring it back to the stable and self-perpetuating status it maintained under a Liberal administration. The measures introduced thus far by the government, designed to curb unemployment have proven insufficient and ineffective, and 90205-6-285i
Unemployment Insurance have failed even to bring to a standstill the alarming process of shrinking of the unemployment insurance fund.
Again I ask how can the unemployment insurance fund subsist when in the Atlantic provinces over 15 per cent to 20 per cent of the labour force is without work? How can it subsist when, as in my own constituency of Gloucester, as of mid-March, the number of unemployed totalled 8,150, representing 55 per cent of our labour force? If the hon. member wishes to know where I obtained these figures, may I say I happen to have the Saint John Tele graph-Journal of Friday, May 5, which carries this headline:
8,150 persons unemployed in Gloucester in midMarch-
$3,783,063 paid in unemployment insurance benefits during year.
Oh, I know the minister will say that most of those applicants for unemployment insurance benefits are fishermen. Well, I ask the minister to read the article and he will find out that this figure includes 750 fishermen and 270 peat moss workers. The minister can take a thousand from the 8,150, if he wants to; he can take off the number of fishermen who are claiming benefits, but the fact will still remain that 50 per cent of the labour force of Gloucester county are unemployed today.
In Gloucester county we have vast possibilities. We have our primary industries of agriculture, lumbering and fishing. We also have one of the largest mineral deposits on this continent. If this government has the intention of protecting and expanding our economy I would ask them to take a good look at our possibilities. I would ask the government to divert part of its northern vision to those areas of New Brunswick where we also have the natural resources which, if brought into production, would add substantially to the general economy of the country and would reduce the number of claimants for unemployment insurance benefits.
Such halfway measures as have been introduced so far this session are not the kind of incentives which are needed to stimulate our economy and to bring the economy of the Atlantic provinces into line with that of other areas of the country. Such measures as the double depreciation scheme, which in the first five months of operation has not produced one single new job, cannot be considered as very effective in stimulating new industries in areas worst affected by present conditions of uncertainty, idleness and confusion.
Enacted in 1940 and coming into operation on July 1, 1941, the Unemployment Insurance Act remains one of the major items of social security legislation in Canada. It embraces almost 75 per cent of our labour force representing over 4 million wage and salary earners

Unemployment Insurance to whom has been paid to date well over $3i billion in benefits. It is a compulsory form of insurance established by the state to afford protection against unemployment if and as long as the insured worker can satisfy certain conditions. In recent years the unemployment insurance fund has become a source of temptation for a government ready for expedients but unprepared and unwilling for fundamental action on its part to assume its share of responsibility.
I therefore move, second by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets the failure of the government to ensure sound administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, resulting in the depletion of the financial resources of the fund and new arbitrary administrative procedures which deny benefits to casual employees."

Mr. Speaker, in my view the amendment placed before the house by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) is a very timely one. I think the fact of the matter is that the unemployment insurance fund has been subjected to pilfering almost to the point of being rendered bankrupt and non-existent. The fact of the matter is that the government, because of its failure to adopt a full employment policy, has made use of the fund for a purpose which was never intended when the act was placed before parliament in 1940.
As I understand the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the unemployment insurance fund it is to provide by way of an insurance measure a sum of money, a fund, credited to the account of an individual and available to that person should he become unemployed under certain circumstances in the future. The purpose of the fund was to take care of that period of time which would ordinarily elapse between the worker losing his present employment and acquiring a new job. The purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act was really to take care of frictional unemployment. Its purpose was to take care of a minimum amount of unemployment and it was designed to provide certain income protection in what was by and large an economy of full employment.
The fund and the plan worked very well as long as we had relatively stable employment, but the fund became endangered and suffered tremendous losses the moment the government failed to maintain something approaching full employment. The government

has gone to the country in a couple of elections on a full employment policy. It has pledged to the people of Canada that it would bring about full employment, that it would maintain full employment, but the unemployment insurance fund is a statistical record of the absolute failure of the government.
In December, 1956, the fund stood at $934 million. That amount had dropped to $874 million by March 31, 1957, and it has been on the way down at a very alarming rate ever since. On March 31, 1958, the fund stood at $744 million. On March 31, 1959, the amount was $499 million, on March 31, 1960, $365 million and on March 31, 1961, $185 million. It is very apparent that unless there is a tremendous improvement in employment in Canada or extraordinary steps are taken by the government the fund will be bankrupt and non-existent in a very short while. The state of the fund demonstrates to all the colossal failure of the government to provide anything approaching a full employment policy.
The government has given a number of excuses why it has been unable to provide full employment. In his baby budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said that one of the reasons for so much unemployment was that so many babies were born in Canada during the war. I have said on other occasions that I have never heard the excuse used before that there are too many babies born in Canada from the standpoint of full employment.
