maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Order, order; if we have fewer interruptions we shall get along faster.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am suggesting that the minister should introduce amendments to the act which would make it possible for those who have been denied benefits to receive them in the future. Those benefits have been available to others in the past. The minister can take the attitude, if he likes, that these people should never be paid. We suggest that they should be paid.
The fund is in a bad way largely because the government has failed to provide full employment, not because of certain misuses of the fund which may exist. This is not the main reason the fund has gone down. Surely all the abuses of the fund about which we have heard did not originate during the period of the Conservative government. It is strange in my opinion that the Canadian people, under a former administration, did not appear to be abusing the fund. If one listens to some hon. gentlemen opposite, one hears that the fund is being raided now by countless people who are abusing it, who have no right to benefits. It is strange that under a Conservative government the people of Canada appear to have lost their morality, according to hon. members opposite, and want to pilfer the fund.
In years gone by, what was the complaint? The complaint from a great many insured workers was that the fund was being built up very rapidly, and that steps should be taken to lower the contributions because the fund was going up and up. Under the Conservative government, the fund has been going down very rapidly. Except for the steps taken in 1959 to increase the contributions by some 30 per cent, when the benefits were increased by only 10 per cent, the fund has continued to go down.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The benefits were never increased.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: There was some slight increase.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
No.

Unemployment Insurance

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East can make his speech when the time comes. The hon. member takes the attitude that the Tories can never do anything right; that they are always wrong in every detail. I think the hon. member for Essex East would make a much stronger case if he were prepared to admit that sometimes hon. gentlemen opposite do introduce certain improvements to certain legislation. The hon. member can deny my statement, but the Canadian Labour Congress made this comparison and said benefits were increased 10 per cent, while contributions from the workers were increased some 30 per cent.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The Canadian Labour Congress made no such statement; I am surprised.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East is an authority on a lot of things but he is not an authority in this case because he is wrong in the statement he has made.
This is not the only way in which the government has brought about a reduction in the fund. There has been mismanagement of the securities in the fund. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) pointed out that the amount of money that had been lost from this fund by this means totalled some $21 million.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: No, over $70 million.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Over $70 million; this represents the amount that has been lost from the fund because of the forced sale of government securities at fire sale prices. We know that at the time of the conversion loan the Minister of Finance twisted the arms of those who have something to do with investments by the unemployment insurance commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: They purchased the reconversion bonds and the fund has been losing money ever since because of the action taken by the government and because of a very depressed bond market at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: A shocking misstatement; perversion of the truth.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I heard that. I suggest that $70 million is pretty expensive, and the fund is down to less than $200 million at the present time. The basic reason that the fund is almost bankrupt is the complete failure of the government to provide anything approaching a full employment policy. If this government maintains its present policy, if it


continues in its failure to meet the unemployment situation, it will foe only a matter of months until the fund will be completely bankrupt.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has been out politicking recently. He was in southwestern Ontario on Saturday when a motion was filed in the government's name but wound up appearing on the order paper in the Prime Minister's name.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: You were in Regina.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I was here Saturday, and I made a few speeches. The Prime Minister was in southwestern Ontario and he was launching something. I am not sure what it was but the press suggests that an election may not be far away because Mr. Frost was with him, and if the Prime Minister is to get any support from the country he will have to lean very heavily on the premier of Ontario. However, the Prime Minister told us that the reason Conservative support in the country was not so good was that the story was not being told of all the government's wonderful legislation; according to him the reason was just a failure to get the story across.
May I say this. The Prime Minister had a northern vision in the last election. The public knows what happened as a result of that vision in the last election. We have had more unemployment than we have had at any time since the 1930's and the unemployment insurance fund is almost depleted. Yet the Prime Minister's answer to this sorry state of affairs is another vision.
I have here a newspaper article which states, in part, "P.M. sets election theme of a new Canada." It was not enough that he had one vision that turned into a nightmare; he is going to have another one. The people of the country cannot afford a second dose of the vision. We cannot afford to keep in office any longer a government that fails to provide full employment and bankrupts the unemployment insurance fund.
We have before us an amendment that we are prepared to support but we should like to move a subamendment. In this subamendment I have pleasure in suggesting that the honourable thing for the government to do is to reimburse the unemployment insurance fund to the extent of the drain that has been brought about by reason of abnormal unemployment with this administration in office. This we suggest is a reasonable thing to do.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: It is the only thing to do.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
The unemployment insurance fund was established in the first place not

as a substitute for full employment but as part of a full employment policy to take care of the 1 per cent, 2 per cent or up to 3 per cent of the labour force that might happen to be unemployed at any given time. In order to maintain the fund, in order to maintain intact the contributions that have been placed in the fund in good faith, we are suggesting that the government should consider reimbursing the fund from the public treasury by the amount that has been lost from excessive unemployment. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin):
That the amendment be amended by deleting the period after the word "employees" and adding thereto the following words:
"and its failure to give consideration to the reimbursement of the fund from the public treasury for the excessive depletion it has suffered as a consequence of the recent abnormal unemployment".
I point out that the subamendment has been carefully drafted so that it should not be interpreted as being a direction to the government to pay funds from the national treasury, something which a private member cannot move; rather, it expresses an opinion of the house, namely that the government should give consideration to the reimbursement of this fund from the public treasury for the excessive depletion it has suffered as a consequence of the recent abnormal unemployment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Unless any hon. member wishes to comment on the proposed amendment to the amendment, I shall place it before the house.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the remarks of the last two speakers, speaking as they were for their parties, we have seen once more a demonstration of the complete irresponsibility of the opposition in this house-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: -and of their absolute failure to do anything -in fact their determination to do absolutely nothing-to assist in the solving of any problems that might be facing this country. Rather, they take their stand, as they have done in the past, in condemning whatever is done without any regard to what might be done to help the situation.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. gentleman has said that opposition groups have taken a position this afternoon only for the purpose of expressing their opposition and not of furthering the interests of the country.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
That is right.
Unemployment Insurance

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: That is what the hon. member has said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that continual interrupter, says "That is true".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Those are unparliamentary words on the part of both the hon. member and the minister and this unintelligent laughter only confirms what I have said.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) allow me to secure a better hearing of his important point of order? I hope hon. members will not interrupt. I am sure all hon. members want to know what the difficulty is.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is contrary to our practice for any hon. member to impute motives. If we in this particular Liberal party take a position and it does not satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite, that does not mean to say that we are not acting in the national interest as we see it.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has made a statement that he should withdraw. It was the kind of statement which was made the other day by the Prime Minister and which should have been withdrawn. Hon. gentlemen opposite continually do this sort of thing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate specifically the imputation which he feels is objectionable.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Obviously Your Honour was preoccupied at the time it was made. The hon. gentleman said that once again the opposition had indicated its irresponsible attitude toward public matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) say "hear, hear". The Secretary of State who is acting responsibly is silent. These gentlemen who hold responsible positions on the government side continue to applaud this remark of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. It is not open to any hon. member to make such imputations. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Minister of Labour to act as a mature and sophisticated member.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
You make me laugh.

Unemployment Insurance

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
It is contrary to the rules of the house to make offensive statements about any hon. member or to impute to any hon. member improper motives. There was a general allegation of irresponsibility directed to the opposite side of politics or the opposite side of the house, as I heard the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), and of motives which perhaps are not desirable but there was no imputation of any immorality and I do not think the remarks go as far as the hon. member suggests they do.
If the hon. member for Essex East were concerned personally and had been named, I would give the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway an opportunity to modify what he said. However, as it was a general allegation I think it is unnecessary to do that.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should point out that the hon. gentleman did refer to two hon. members. He referred particularly to the last two speakers, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). Then the hon. member made a general comment of an umbrella kind which would include others.
I say to you, sir, with great respect, that those were improper words and should not be allowed to rest without being challenged by the Chair.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: I am sorry; I cannot agree with the hon. member. Will the hon. member continue.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to clear up this matter at once. I was not insinuating that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) or the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) are any more irresponsible than other hon. members of the opposition.
If there were any unintentional slight on those hon. members I would certainly be prepared to modify that.
We have heard a barrage of complaints about the unemployment insurance fund being depleted. I think this is a serious problem facing the country and the government, and the government has recognized that by indicating its intention to bring forward at this session of parliament amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: They should have been brought in months ago.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I
should think the fact that the government has stated its intention well in advance of bringing forward legislation gives the opposition and anybody who is willing to contribute to
[Mr. Starr.)

the solution of the problem an opportunity to bring forward suggestions as to how it should be done.
However, as usual the opposition have failed to take that up; they have failed completely to offer any suggestions except the one suggestion that they make on all problems that face Canada, that we should print some more money and pay it out of the federal treasury. That seems to solve everything in their view. Perhaps if we make a few more printing presses and print money faster we will be able to solve all problems on the basis upon which they want to solve them.
Then they turn around and tell us that the fund is going down very quickly; it is going to be bankrupt and we are going to face very dire consequences. Immediately they get past that point they complain, not that we are paying out too much money but that we are not paying out enough. They tell us that many people are being deprived of their right to draw from the fund and all kinds of people are being deprived of proper benefit.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am
not suggesting more people should not be covered by the act and should benefit, but I hope I have enough responsibility to offer some suggestion as to how this can be brought about other than by printing more money.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Provide more employment. Give them the work the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) promised.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Yes, we had some great suggestions for creating employment in this country from the opposition, but-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: We had wonderful ones from the Prime Minister in 1958.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
-I
suggest that if all the working people are to be covered by the act, it must be put on a proper, paying basis. Unemployment insurance has been the greatest protection the working man has enjoyed not only in this country but throughout the world.
Many of the people who have studied this subject in great detail have come to the conclusion that unemployment does occur from time to time in all countries of the world, and it has occurred for the past 600 years. We are not likely to stop it overnight.
I notice that in a publication by Louis Pink entitled "Freedom from fear" it is said: After 60 years of experience, Great Britain has decided that their unemployment insurance system must remain the major method of meeting unemployment.

I could go on to quote many other statements in this regard. My very strong feeling is that if the Unemployment Insurance Act is amended along lines which will provide adequate protection for the unemployed of this country, it will at the same time do a great deal to alleviate unemployment.
Some time ago I gave notice of a motion to the house in connection with amendments which I felt should be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act, but because of the business of the house it was not possible to bring that motion forward.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Thank goodness for that.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I
should like to suggest to the government that these amendments to the act be considered. The resolution I placed on the order paper under date of January 31 was as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for recognition of the principle that every employable person in the labour force is entitled either to a job or to adequate compensation by including the following provisions:
(a)	The act should be renamed the unemployment compensation act.
(b)	Every person in the labour force who is employed under a contract of service should contribute to the fund regardless of income or occupation.
(c)	Every insured person in the labour force-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Order. Before the hon. member goes any further, while I do not like to circumscribe his contribution to the debate I feel that if he is allowed to present his resolution as relevant it will be relevant to debate the propositions which are contained in it, thereby enlarging the scope of this debate very substantially.
At the present time the grievance expressed in the amendment concerns the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the results of that administration. This has been extended to a complaint about the failure of the government to consider the reimbursement of the fund. So that only in so far as the hon. member's proposals are relevant to the administration and the reimbursement of the fund would I consider it proper for him to continue.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that the government has announced its intention to bring forward amendments to the act indicates that in order to be able to administer the act properly it does require amendment. The situation which has arisen at the present time makes it impossible to administer it properly, and with the paying out within the terms of the act that is being done, nothing could happen to the fund but its depletion.
Unemployment Insurance
It then becomes a question of how the fund should be built up. The opposition have suggested, as I say, that the federal government should simply contribute a large amount of money to reimburse the fund. I am suggesting that if the act is changed in a proper way, that will not be necessary.
I think it is unsound for the federal government to just pay a huge sum of money into the fund. I think this act must be put on a proper, paying basis. If it is ever going to be administered properly by anybody, it has to be on a sound and paying basis. That is the reason I suggest these amendments to the act, because I believe many people now drawing out of the fund should not be drawing out of it, and many people who should be able to qualify to draw out of the fund are not now qualified to draw out of it, nor do they pay into it.
With your concurrence, Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue putting these suggested amendments before the house. I think you will find they are relevant to what has been suggested by the opposition. They would provide a much better means of administering the act and putting it on a sound basis than has been suggested by the opposition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am asking the hon. member to use his own discretion about what parts of his own resolution are relevant rather than putting in all of his proposals.
I admit there may be some relevance in some of his proposals, but others would bring about a quite broad extension of this debate, which would be quite unwarranted.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have heard suggestions by the hon. member for Gloucester about fishermen. There have been a great many protests throughout the country about fishermen drawing from this fund when they are certain to be unemployed during the winter months.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: They are not certain to be unemployed.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
That
has been a complaint made about many of the seasonal industries, that there really is not a risk of insurance when they are certain to be unemployed. I have not supported that view. I have at all times felt that these benefits should apply to every person in this country who is ready, willing and able to work. They should be covered by the act. This, of course, has not been done up to the present time, for various reasons.
There are some groups, such as civil servants, which are not included under the act. I believe they should be. It is argued that these people are in permanent employment
4518	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance but that has not turned out to be the case on all occasions. I notice that in a television program a couple of months ago it was stated that a number of employees of the city of Ottawa had been laid off. They were not liable for benefit because it had been presumed they were in permanent employment.
In the case of civil servants, both federal and provincial, there are many temporary employees. The provinces can use their discretion as to which of their employees shall be subject to the provisions of the act and, of course, they follow the policy of insuring those people who are temporary employees and who are almost certain to draw benefit at one time or another. I feel, therefore, that these classes of employees are not bearing their share of the cost of unemployment insurance. Either no civil servants should be covered or all of them should be covered. As I have said before, I believe this applies not only to civil servants but to all those employed under contract of service.
I firmly believe that those who are going to benefit from the act should be the ones who are required to contribute to it. That does not appear to be the policy of the opposition. If the federal government is going to contribute huge sums to the unemployment insurance fund, as they suggest, we would be taking the money out of general taxation. Among those contributing to its payment would then be persons in receipt of old age pensions and elderly people who could not possibly receive any benefit from the fund and who therefore, I submit, have no reason to be paying into it. A solution such as is suggested by the opposition would obviously require a higher level of taxation. I submit that we have to amend the act in such a way as to protect those who need protection and provide for them for as long as they need such assistance without regard to the number of contributions they have made to the fund.
There has been a good deal of talk in the country about returning to insurance principles in this act. However, as I pointed out on a previous occasion, everyone has a different idea as to what constitutes insurance principles. I pointed out that in the case of fire insurance, for example, if a person's house burns down he receives the entire amount that is necessary to rebuild the house or to build another. In the case of unemployment insurance, however, this principle does not apply because a person only receives benefit in direct relationship to what he has paid into the fund. I do not believe that the individual in this country is in any position to accept a risk of that sort himself. For these reasons


I believe contributions must be spread over the entire labour force. I disagree with the views which have been expressed by the opposition. If we go beyond spreading the cost among the labour force, we begin to spread it among the entire population of the country. It seems to me that the people who are in a position to pay into the fund are the people who are gainfully employed.
Some suggestion has been made that proper protection has not been provided by the government for the people who are paying contributions. I suggest that this is no fault of the government but that it follows from the terms of the act itself. People are drawing money out of the fund who should not be drawing it out, but although there have been many fraudulent claims, as we would all agree, I do not think this represents the serious problem which some people make it out to be.
However, I do believe there are many married women drawing money out of the fund who have absolutely no need to do so. It is very difficult to establish whether or not married women are actually looking for jobs. This is one of the things which, in my view, is helping to drain the fund. Certainly, it is beyond the ability of government to control this practice by way of administration; an amendment of the act is required in order to deal with things of this nature.
Another cause of huge drains on the fund is the action of people who retire at the age of 65 and who then feel qualified to draw from the fund for 52 weeks. Though they only represent 3 per cent of the claims on the fund they are responsible for 10 per cent of the money paid out.
Then again, because of the unemployment situation, the government decided to extend, for a month at either end, the seasonal benefits. Some might wish to criticize the government for making this decision but personally I feel that it should have been made, that it was properly made, and that the contribution which the government makes to the fund even under the present financial arrangements is more than adequate to cover the administration of the fund and anything paid out in seasonal benefits. For this reason I feel criticism of the government on this ground is unjustified.
May I call it six o'clock?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house took recess at six o'clock I had been dealing in general terms with the amendment and subamendment moved by the two opposition parties condemning the government's administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and indicating I felt that this condemnation was entirely without foundation. I believe there are many reasons why it is without foundation, but I do not think we can find a better authority for this statement than the hon. member for Gloucester who moved the amendment, because, in the course of his own remarks, he indicated that in his view the reason that the unemployment insurance fund had been depleted was that there was a high number of claimants drawing benefits from the fund. With that statement I certainly agree. He did not blame the condition of the fund on the high unemployment particularly, as the subamendment does; he simply blamed it on the high number of claimants drawing from the fund. I think this is an accurate statement and a complete denial of the amendment which he subsequently moved.
I believe, as I had started to indicate before the dinner recess, that there are a number of reasons why there are a high number of claimants under the act. We have the case of married women. It was pointed out by Dr. Warren James that 85 per cent of the married women were at one time or another claimants under the fund, and that in most instances when they did go on unemployment insurance they exhausted the entire amount of their benefits and that it was very difficult indeed to establish whether those women were desirous of finding work or were in fact, ready, willing and able to work. In most instances it was also shown that they had husbands who were working full-time and for that reason there really was not any necessity for their drawing funds under the act.
As I pointed out, those who retired at age 65 and drew benefits for a year were responsible for 3 per cent of the claims under the act but drew 10 per cent of the total benefits paid out under the act. I indicated the action the government had taken to increase the amount of benefit under the act and also to extend the seasonal benefit period. This was done because of the unemployment situation. These are some of the things that have led to the depletion of the unemployment insurance fund. However, it is quite clear from a consideration of those facts that the administration of the act itself has absolutely nothing to do with its depletion. Therefore,
Unemployment Insurance as I have said, on his own words, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gloucester falls to the ground. It is absolutely and completely without any substantiation.
The hon. member did complain about losses suffered by the investment committee, but he did not put that forward as a major cause of the unemployment insurance fund being depleted. He also neglected to point out that while some losses had been incurred in the investments there never at any time was an over-all loss to the fund from investment of the unemployment insurance funds. There never has been a year when there has not been a substantial profit made from the investments in securities made by the unemployment insurance investment committee, and I am sure no one would want to hold the investment committee responsible for an error in judgment in sustaining a loss on one particular transaction. No investment committee in this country is infallible and I do not suppose we are ever likely to have one that is. However, I believe, over all, the investment policy has proved to be a sound one and has worked to the benefit of the fund.
The solution proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia is to condemn the government for failure to give consideration to the reimbursement of the fund from the public treasury. Well, I do not know how he is in a position to say to what the government has or has not given consideration. Perhaps he knows more about what the cabinet considers than the rest of us do, but I have not known the cabinet to make public those things which they are considering or are not considering unless they have made a specific decision on it and have said they have considered it and rejected it, and I know of no such statement being made by the government. Therefore, 1 fail to see how he is in a position to condemn the government for failure to give consideration to this measure.
The hon. member might want to condemn them for not doing it. If that is so, I quite agree with the government if it is their decision not to reimburse the fund from public moneys because I do not believe it should be done. If, as I have said, the depletion of the fund has been brought about by people drawing from it who should not be drawing from it, it is not in a sound position and the pumping of public money into it will do absolutely nothing to correct the situation. It would continue in the same way it has in the past. If we put $100 million into it, it would simply be drawn off by people who should not be drawing benefits from the fund. For this reason I believe there must be far more substantial amendments to the act.
The hon. member for Gloucester raised several points, one of which I started to deal

Unemployment Insurance with earlier, namely the question of seasonal employees drawing benefits from the fund. He was of the view that they should continue to draw from the fund, and I have taken the same view. I believe all people should draw from it but I also take the view that they should all contribute. Of course, this is where the difficulty arises at the present time. I pointed out that in the instance of the civil service, only those who draw from the fund are registered under it. Those who are employed steadily do not pay into the fund. It is perfectly obvious that if this fund is to be sustained at all it has to be done on a proper basis with everybody who is gainfully employed contributing to the fund.
The other question that arises in regard to seasonal employees is that there is no limitation placed on the amount of earnings they can have in a year. Therefore, in actual fact, we may have a seasonal employee who pays into the fund for eight months and then draws benefits for four months although he may have earned in that eight months more than another man who has worked for the entire 12 months and has been forced to pay into the fund for 12 months. I believe this is a very unfair and unsound situation. For this reason I believe some limitation must be placed on the amount of earnings that a person can have in a year and still draw benefits from the fund. I do not suggest this in the form of a means test, because what I consider to be a means test would deal with assets. I do not believe we should take into consideration anything that a man has, such as a house, and so on.
I believe my suggestion would help a great deal those people who are now meeting a means test. It would help to overcome that problem if everybody was covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act and was paid benefits for so long as he was out of work regardless of the amount of contribution he had paid into the fund. Because we already look after these people in one way or another at the present time, I suggest that there would be no greater cost involved in that if a person's benefits expire today he then goes on unemployment assistance or some other form of relief under which he has to meet a means test. I do not believe that should be the case in this country. I believe every person is entitled either to a job or to adequate compensation if he is out of work through no fault of his own and provided he is ready, willing and able to accept a job.
In order to accomplish this end and keep the cost at a reasonable level, I believe there must be certain limitations placed upon the act. I believe that a person who has earned $4,000 or over in a particular year has


no need to draw benefits from the fund in that year although if the same person were out of work in the following year there would be no limitation on the amount he could draw. He would be able to draw for the entire year if he were out of work but I do not think a person who has had an income in excess of $4,000 in a year needs to benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act in that year.
Neither do I believe that married women whose husbands are working full-time and are adequately able to support them have any need to draw from the fund. Again, I noticed in the unemployment statistics a short while ago that almost half of the unemployed in the country were between 14 and 19 years of age. I believe adequate provision is made by the federal government for training these people if they are unable to find employment. If they have not got the proper skills to find employment, I believe the place for them is in school and I do not think they should be on the labour market or benefiting under the Unemployment Insurance Act. As long as they are living at home with parents who are adequately able to provide for them, having in mind that the government is making provision for them to take vocational training or whatever other kind of training may be necessary to fit them for a job, I believe that is what they should be doing instead of drawing on the unemployment insurance fund with no action being taken to ensure that they will ever be able to earn a living for themselves.
I also believe the act in general needs to be tightened up because I think there is a good deal of collusion between employers and employees with respect to people quitting their jobs when there is no need to do so and then drawing unemployment insurance. I believe there should be severe penalties imposed on any employee or employer acting separately or in collusion to defraud the fund. Again, I find that when I ask people why they felt they were entitled to do certain things under the Unemployment Insurance Act the answer I often get is that everybody else is doing it and it is all right in their opinion and they feel they would be foolish not to draw benefits, although in my view they are not entitled to draw them. They seem to come within the terms of the act. Those things which constitute fraud upon the fund should be clearly set out and there should be severe penalties imposed on those people who do attempt to defraud the fund.
I see that my time is drawing to a close. I do wish to emphasize that the negative attitude perpetually taken by members of the opposition in the house is not going to solve any of the problems of the country. It is no

use condemning perpetually. They always seem to be against something. I have not heard a helpful suggestion come from them during the whole time I have been here.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the matter now being discussed, and I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), particularly his reference to unemployment insurance for fishermen. From time to time one hears the criticism that unemployment insurance for fishermen is the reason or a reason why the unemployment insurance fund is being depleted. Surprisingly enough, some of these criticisms are made by representatives of commercial interests who in Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces as a whole have a captive market. However, I do not think these opinions are shared by any hon. member of the house.
I certainly do not agree with the speaker who preceded me, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), in his suggestion that hon. members on this side of the house are other than responsible and constructive in their criticism, but I noticed that he too subscribed to the idea of unemployment insurance for fishermen. The fact is that unemployment insurance for fishermen was a very constructive step that was taken in order to assist the fishermen, a class of workers who seriously need and deserve unemployment insurance. It has proved to be a real blessing to the fishermen themselves and I am quite sure that indirectly it has made a contribution to steadying the economy of the Atlantic provinces as well as having made a contribution to the economy of Canada as a whole.
In discussing the matter of the administration of the unemployment insurance fund, I should like to say at the outset that I make a distinction between abuses involving the drawing of unemployment insurance unfairly
Unemployment Insurance and unnecessary hardship caused to a class of workers who suffer under the administration of the act because, rightly or wrongly, there are many instances where workers such as carpenters, handymen, artisans and others who are employed by individuals find that at the end of their working period they do not qualify for unemployment insurance. In that connection I should like to read a letter from a constituent of mine which sets forth his own experience and in doing so tells the story very well as to what has happened to those men who depend upon casual labour for their livelihood and who find that such work is not insurable. The letter is from Roland J. Menchenton of Norris Arm North Side in the constituency of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. The letter was written early in January and reads as follows:
I am going to state what happened to us this past summer. Myself, Bennet White and William Freake, all of Norris Arm North, was employed at Grand Falls this past summer. Myself and Mr. William Freake built a house for Mr. Robert Malloy, No. 9 Station Road, Grand Falls. We received $1.75 per hour and received ten unemployment stamps for this job. We then went to work for Mr. John Malloy, same address, for three weeks. After job was completed we were informed by the unemployment insurance commission that there was a new law in effect which stated that no person outside of a bona fide contractor or employer could buy stamps. Result was we did not get any. We then went to work with Mr. George Peercey and worked with him six weeks with the same result. We also worked with Mr. Robert Piercey (both of Grand Falls) for three weeks and were told that it was not insurable work under the new law. Result was after working since middle of June until December 20 we were unable to qualify for regular insurance and did not have the required stamps for seasonal benefit.
Now, sir, one half of the work done in the town of Grand Falls is done by men like ourselves, two or three men on a job. And now we are denied the privilege of buying stamps. Now what, may I ask, is going to happen to the hundreds of workers like ourselves who find employment in this way? Do we after working steady for 25 or 30 weeks have to spend the few dollars we have managed to save or as in the case of the majority fall back on able bodied relief. To my mind there could have been a law made to offset the illegal claims made on the unemployment insurance commission without taking away the rights and privileges of the honest workers who try to earn a livelihood without being a burden on the government in the form of able bodied relief.
I think the quotations from that letter depict one of the problems which faces workers who depend upon short term employment. It is causing a great deal of unrest and a great deal of hardship in the long run, and is one reason why we are making these criticisms at this time. The hon. member who preceded me charged us on this side of the house with criticizing only and making no constructive suggestions. I, of course, deny that allegation. However, I have yet to find a constructive

Unemployment Insurance suggestion made by those on this side which has been listened to by hon. members on the other side.
The suggestion which I would make now is that an amendment be made to this act which would permit the act to be applied in the way in which it was originally intended to be applied, that is to give assistance where assistance is needed. This act should be insurance against unemployment for all people out of work who want to work, who do not try to avoid work. This was the real motive behind the passing of the act. Apart from being of help in a practical way to those who are out of work, this insurance principle has the additional advantage of cushioning periods of recession and unemployment such as the one through which we are going at the present time. Undoubtedly a tightening up of the act, a restriction in its application, is a denial of the very principles upon which the act was founded.
I do hope the suggestions we are making now that the act be applied fairly to those deserving of assistance, those who are out of work through no fault of their own and who should be insurable, will be given careful consideration by those who sit opposite.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we find the opposition introducing an amendment to a motion to go into supply under a guise that is purposely designed to permit them to make an attack on government policy with regard to employment in this country. There is little that can be said by way of commendation of this particular amendment. I believe hon. members of the opposition find themselves on the horns of a dilemma. In one breath they criticize and attack the government for its administration of the fund, and the resultant depletion of the fund, and in the next breath they attack the government for taking measures to restrict abuses being made of the fund. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. They place themselves in a directly contradictory position.
For three years now, the members of the opposition have been talking in terms of depression and recession. Both in this house and throughout the country, they have decried the fact that we have unemployment. They have used unemployment as the basis for introducing amendment after amendment, and on occasion they have even attempted to adjourn the business of this house to discuss unemployment as a matter of urgent public importance. Time and time again, they have talked in terms of hundreds of thousands being unemployed. As a matter of fact, on one occasion, they even referred to one million. Now they come along and ask what has


happened to the fund. One sometimes wonders, when observing them in action, what they are thinking. They make no suggestions about what we should do or what should be done. They have not suggested the things we have not done. On the one hand, they accuse us of doing nothing in the face of high unemployment, and on the other hand they say the fund should not have been used to alleviate the problems created by unemployment or the hardships that result from unemployment.
They suggest the fund should not be used for the purpose for which we presume it was intended. One wonders how they are going to get out of this dilemma. They refer to $900 million being in the fund in 1957. One wonders, Mr. Speaker, if the establishment of the unemployment insurance fund in this country was nothing more than a piece of Liberal party window dressing. In the first instance, they say unemployment is high. If they say unemployment is high, then they must admit that the fund which was intended to deal with unemployment was used in the way in which it was intended to be used. They do not accuse us of wasting the fund for if they did, they would then definitely be saying that the fund should not be used for any purpose whatever. The one argument destroys the other. If the opposition protests against what I am saying this evening, then they are saying that the passage of the act itself was nothing more than a pure farce, a simple device for window dressing and never intended for anything other than political propaganda.
The action we have taken in respect of the fund, Mr. Speaker, is similar to the action now being taken in the United States under parallel circumstances. At the time of the recession, we extended seasonal benefits. We made the formula more flexible. We brought married women under the act so that there would not be any discrimination and to assist in increasing family income. As the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) pointed out, we brought fishermen under the act.

I wish to deal now with the second half of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Gloucester. I have here a draft statement which was prepared by the unemployment insurance commission in connection with the changes that were made. Perhaps in the interests of clarity, and so there will be no misunderstanding, I should read the statement at this time:
Recently there had been complaints regarding the cancellation of stamps purchased by registered
Unemployment Insurance and non-registered employers alike and also regarding the withdrawal of the privilege to certain employers, who are not required to register with the unemployment insurance commission, to purchase unemployment insurance stamps.
These complaints stem from the fact that employers have been insuring persons who are not properly insurable. These persons fall into two main categories. First, those whose employment was not under a contract of service; and second, those who were employed on a casual basis for other than the employer's trade or business.
Referring to the first group, Mr. Speaker, section 25 (a) of the Unemployment Insurance Act provides that employment is insurable when it is:
*-employment in Canada, by one or more employers, under any express or implied contract of service or apprenticeship, written or oral, whether the earnings of the employed person are received from the employer or some other person and whether the earnings are reckoned by time or by the piece, or partly by time and partly by the piece, or otherwise.
The statement continues:
The civil code of Quebec does not use the expression "contract of service" but the arrangement is much the same as what the civil code calls "lease and hire of personal services" as distinguished from "work done by estimate and contract".
The contract of service is an agreement, written or oral, under which the relationship between the employer and the employed person is substantially that of master and servant. The essentials in such a contract are that one person engaging the services of another must have the right to:
(a)	tell him not only what result he, the employer, wants produced but also the time when, the place where, and the precise way in which the work is to be done;
(b)	require that the worker do the work personally, unlike an independent contractor who can and often does delegate it to a substitute or employee of his own;
(c)	to terminate the worker's services at any time. Likewise the employee may quit his employment without being compelled to specific performance of his contract.
The significant factor of a contract of service is the right of the hirer to control the hired. It will be seen at once that without such a control an employed person would be more or less his own boss and when it came to the payment of benefit the question of whether he was unemployed or not would be difficult, if not impossible, to determine.
The unemployment insurance commission found that many persons were being insured as employees when in fact they were independent contractors, partners, members of family undertakings, joint entrepreneurs, co-adventurers and such like.
With respect to casual employment the statement reads:
Referring to the second group, section 27 (p) of the Unemployment Insurance Act specifically excludes from insurability "employment of a casual nature otherwise than for the employer's trade or business".
In the early days of its existence the commission, by an administrative ruling, defined casual employment as employment of not more than ten days' duration within a 30-day period. This was later reduced to employment of not more than six days'

Unemployment Insurance
duration in a 30-day period. Thus employment of a duration of more than ten days-and later, more than six days-was determined insurable.
The commission through a regulation authorized employers of such casual help to purchase stamps on making application to the post office, thus waiving the necessity for the employer to first register with the commission.
On February 3, 1961, the umpire, who is the final authority in the interpretation of the Unemployment Insurance Act, ruled that any casual employment of a non-continuing nature, when performed for other than an employer's trade or business, was not insurable. This of course nullified the commission's administrative ruling and at the same time did away with the necessity for providing for the purchase of stamps on application at post offices by non-registered employers.
It should be pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that this ruling is the same as that which is applied to the workmen's compensation acts of the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia, as well as in Great Britain.
The statement continues:
Unfortunately, the facts concerning these two types of employment are not determinable in the vast majority of cases until audits are carried out or claims filed or investigations made. Once the facts come to light the commission has no option but to cancel the contributions erroneously made and adjust any benefits paid on the basis of these contributions.
However, in view of the fact that special instructions to offices of the commission regarding contract of service were issued on September 27,
1960,	and the umpire's decision regarding casual employment was handed down only on February 3,
1961,	no overpayment of benefit will be established in relation to contributions made in cases involving either of these factors prior to the two respective dates mentioned, provided, of course, the commission is satisfied there was no misrepresentation.
I might add, in addition to what the statement contained, that audits and investigations of casual purchases of stamps have revealed that fraud was rampant. Purchases were made where no work was done at all. Stamps were being purchased in excess of the actual employment period and exchanges of labour, whereby A employed B for a period, then B employed A in turn until both had sufficient contributions to qualify for benefit were not uncommon.
In reply to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) who made some glib references to a full employment policy when speaking in this debate earlier, it is true, of course, that he made full use of his time to attack the government on its employment policies. I do not propose to deal at any length with what he said but I should like to refer to the full employment policy of the socialist group who sit, Mr. Speaker, on your immediate left. Full employment must mean something or it means nothing at all. In the sense in which the group who sit over in that corner mean it, it means nothing less than regimentation. You can guarantee employment in this country through the use of

socialist methods; you can do it if you want to fix wages; you can do it if you want to fix prices.

In order to make their system work we are bound to have total regimentation. We are bound to have to tell people where they are to work, how long they are to work and how much they are to receive for their labour. We will be bound to tell industry what products to produce and what prices they are to receive for those products; we will be bound to tell the farmers of this country what to produce on their farms and to tell them what they will receive for the fruits of their labour. I call this totalitarianism.

Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to congratulate the hon. member for Gloucester for the constructive and brilliant way with which he dealt with unemployment insurance problems. I am sure that he has made it clear to a good many citizens that persons who are concerned over the situation of the unemployment insurance fund can still be found in this house.
He also made it clear to others who are deprived of unemployment benefits as a result of amendments to the act that there are still people here in this house who want to cooperate so that the government may review those amendments that we consider intolerable.
In fact, the hon. member for Gloucester introduced the following amendment:
This house regrets the failure of the government to ensure sound administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, resulting in the depletion of the financial resources of the fund and new arbitrary administrative procedures which deny benefits to casual employees.
I believe that the hon. member for Gloucester has adequately dealt with the position of the fund.
As for me, I would especially like to deal with the arbitrary procedures which deny benefits to casual employees.
Therefore, I should like to refer to Hansard for February 9, 1961, on page 1050. On that occasion I put the following question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr):
I should like to put a question to the Minister of Labour. In view of the many complaints voiced by unemployed who are no longer drawing unemployment insurance benefits because of the new interpretation given to the service contract, does the minister intend to issue further instructions in order to remedy a situation that has become impossible?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member gave me notice that he would ask this question. I immediately contacted the unemployment insurance commission, and they advise me that there is no new interpretation of the regulations with regard to the contract of service. The difference now is, so they tell me, that the regulations are being enforced.
A little later, as it can be seen on the same page, I asked the following supplementary question:

Unemployment Insurance
Mr. Speaker, in view of the answer just given by the Minister of Labour I would like to ask him whether he is aware that the enforcement of the instructions now contained in pamphlet 13, where the commission defines "service contract", is detrimental to the campaign for winter works, particularly in the renovation and home construction field.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am not aware that it is having the effect which the hon. member says it is.
Mr. Speaker, those questions and answers were given on February 9, 1961 but if you refer to the L'Action Catholique of January 13, 1961, you will find the following item:
Details given by the unemployment insurance commission.
In order to spare the people of Canada some of the difficulties which now prevail throughout the country, the unemployment insurance commission wishes to caution people regarding the eligibility to insurance benefits of casual and family employment.
In view of recent decisions, the unemployment insurance commission arbitrator, Mr. Justice J. D. Kearney, has issued new interpretations concerning the eligibility of workers holding family and casual jobs.
Family employment: In most family concerns, where some or all the employees are related to the owner, there is no real master-servant relationship. This form of enterprise rather suggests that the family relationship supersedes or annuls the service contract. In many other cases, the several members of the family are working toward a common objective, and the profit is shared according to certain needs or as the owner sees fit.
Mr. Chairman, I come to the part dealing specifically with circular No. 13:
Casual employment: Again in that classification, the majority of employees are not insurable since a service contract does not exist within meaning of the unemployment insurance act.
I am now talking about casual employment.
For a service contract to exist, the casual employer must be in a position to control and supervise the technical performance of the work to be carried out by the employed. Since most of casual employees work alone, the fact that the salary is paid hourly, per unit of work, or according to contract is of no importance, those employees are considered as working for themselves and their employment is not insurable.
Before entering contributions in unemployment insurance stamp books of people holding casual or family employment, employers should inquire at their local office, to prevent possible cancellation of those stamps later on.
Well, the ruling of the U.I.C. arbitrator, Mr. Justice J. D. Kearney, is rather at variance with the answer given by the minister to the question I put to him on February 9, since Mr. Justice Kearney himself agrees that since September 27, the date shown on bulletin No 13, the unemployment insurance commission has issued new interpretations concerning the eligibility of casual employees. Therefore, if the letter of the act was not

changed, its interpretation at least was changed, and that is the important thing in the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Mr. Speaker, this circular letter No. 13, which was issued September 27, 1960, applies retroactively to the year 1960. The pamphlet deals with the service contract and, among other things, includes the following definition:
Employment in Canada, by one or more employers, under a service or apprenticeship contract, whether explicit or implicit, written or oral, whether the earnings of the employee are received from the employer or someone else, and whether calculated by the hour or by the piece, or partly by the hour and partly by the piece, or otherwise.
But, more interesting still is the type of questions asked by certain officers of unemployment insurance offices in order to determine whether there is a service contract or not between the employer and the employee. Here, for instance, is the series of questions that are asked:
Starting date?
Termination date?
Where was the above-mentioned person employed by you?
Was he paid certain wages or hired on contract?
If wages, state if hourly, daily or weekly?
What salary were you paying him?
Who fixed his salary?
What is your main occupation?
What did he do for you?
What was your reason for hiring him?
In what capacity was he employed?
What experience did you have in the type of work he performed for you?
Were you present on site at the time the work was done?
Were you working yourself?
Who kept his time record?
Have you kept track of his time?
What were the agreed working hours?
Mr. Speaker, all those questions may deprive a worker from qualifying for the contributions provided under the Unemployment Insurance Act. For instance, I have already mentioned in the house that when an individual is hired to build a house, it is ridiculous for unemployment insurance officers to ask him the purpose of his employment. It is obvious that he was employed to build the house.
Another question is: "What knowledge did you have of the type of work he performed for you?" Again I ask, must one be a carpenter to hire carpenters to build a house and to affix the appropriate unemployment insurance stamps in their books?
This is also true of the following question:
Did you remain on the premises while the work was being performed?
That is another question that can lead to confusion and deprive some workers of contributions to which they are entitled. It is

well known that if a person who hires a carpenter is not qualified to supervise his work and knows nothing about carpentry, he will seldom remain on the premises to tell a qualified worker what he should do.
In a number of constituencies, hundreds of unemployed people are deprived of benefits they should receive, merely because officers of the commission have been instructed to give a new interpretation to the term "work contract". Personally, I know of many families which are suffering real hardship and have to depend on relief.
Following that new interpretation, the unemployment insurance commission people are always bringing up the same argument, namely that the employer must have enough authority for giving orders and enough competence for directing the work of one or several employees. That is a false interpretation which is subject to contradiction every day. As a matter of fact, few employers know more than their employees. A contractor is not necessarily a carpenter, bricklayer, electrician, stonemason, etc., but he employs qualified people in those various trades. Yet, those employees are eventually entitled to benefits, because they have been working for a contractor. An industrialist often knows little or nothing about the complex structure of his business. Yet, all his employees are entitled to unemployment insurance.
Many a citizen retains the services of tradesmen for certain casual repairs or extensions to their properties. Working conditions are agreed upon verbally. But, since circular No. 13 has been in force, no such employee or worker qualifies for unemployment insurance benefits.
In my riding, as in many others, all trades people and labourers who work for employers other than registered contractors are struck from the list of those qualified to receive benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Finally, it seems that, in order to replenish the unemployment insurance fund, officials are creating misery and desolation among our working population. That is the greatest shame at this time, and we will certainly not give up fighting for our workers.
If clause 25 of the Unemployment Insurance Act under its present form can be so fantastically interpreted, it should be better defined, so as not to deprive an honest worker of unemployment insurance benefits, to which he was formerly entitled.
Unemployment Insurance
To my mind, this is not a question of politics, but a matter of justice, and the workers are now aware of the extent to which they are being slighted.
If it had only been a matter of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act it would not have been so bad. But, on the contrary, the amendment was made retroactive, so that employers, who had honestly and legally affixed unemployment insurance stamps in their workers' books, and the workers themselves, who had legally and honestly paid their contributions, are being deprived of benefits, because of the attitude of the unemployment insurance commission.
Yet, those employers and employees have made those contributions and that is not all. Those employees applied to the unemployment insurance office after September 26, 1960, with the impression that they were entitled to draw benefits, as they were indeed under the act. Today, they find themselves in an impossible situation as a result of the retroactivity decreed in circular No. 13.
As I was saying that amendment may have been introduced in order to protect the unemployment insurance fund, and we have every reason to believe that this was the original purpose. But it seems to me the government or the unemployment insurance commission should have considered the consequences that this new rule might have, not only on the unemployment insurance fund itself but also on the administration of the act in relation to both employees and employers.
In addition to what I have just mentioned, that circular eliminates almost all cases of insurability for casual and seasonal jobs. In the past, unemployment insurance officials used to make rulings on the insurability of jobs, while today they have to enquire whether or not there is a service contract. Employers are dissatisfied with such a procedure, in so far as the supervision of certain jobs is concerned, such as the building of private homes, logging operations, etc.
Of course, the workers too are dissatisfied, particularly the many labourers in rural areas who were formerly employed in housing construction and were paid hourly wages. They are being deprived of their rights and are being discriminated against if you compare their situation to that of employees working for contractors. In fact, those who cannot find a job with a contractor will have no

Unemployment Insurance protection whatsoever in view of the interpretation given to section 25 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Such an interpretation is a serious impediment to the carrying out of certain repair jobs during the summer season, because in the case of repairs to private homes, the employment of workers and carpenters is not covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I listened closely to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Gloucester. He mentioned, among other things, that the poor condition of the unemployment insurance fund was due in part to poor management and to speculation on certain bonds. It is unfortunate that the money in the fund, most of which, that is to say 80 per cent, had been contributed by the employers and employees, was endangered through poor investments. The hon. member for Gloucester also emphasized the need to replenish the unemployment insurance fund. He particularly urged the government to provide work for the unemployed. I think that is the best way of avoiding the payment of benefits, and those who find a job will only feel the better for it.
I was reading this afternoon on page 1403 of Hansard for January 25, 1961, a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) in which be quoted the Prime Minister as saying-this was on August 30, 1958-that legislation would be introduced to extend the period of entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits and make such benefits available to certain classes of farm workers.
Mr. Speaker, that is another vision that will have to be set aside, because as long as certain workers and labourers are denied unemployment insurance benefits, it is silly to believe that the Prime Minister would now consider extending them to certain classes of farm workers.
The hon. parliamentary secretary told us a few moments ago that certain provisions had been adopted with regard to unemployment insurance which, in his opinion, were designed to favour the workers. He mentioned, among others, the extension of the unemployment insurance benefits period. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house, cannot blame the government for extending the period of unemployment insurance benefits, especially at a time when there are so many unemployed in this country. But it was not a measure designed to provide work to Canadian workers; it was rather designed


to put a poultice on a peg leg, since all it does is to provide, certain workers for a certain period with the opportunity to receive unemployment insurance benefits. Unfortunately no later than May 15 those who are now favoured by extension of the benefits period will find themselves in the same position as those who cannot get them any more because of the service contract amendment.
It is true that certain amendments have been made to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Among others according to the pamphlet published by the unemployment insurance commission and bearing No. UIC 651 E GO-59) we see, for instance, that in 1959, amendments to the act were made concerning woodsmen. Well, these new regulations, I believe, have been quite prejudicial to woodsmen. For instance, the amendment to the regulations causes a more widespread use of power saws, which results in a larger weekly production than before. Among other things, the unemployment insurance commission mentioned in this pamphlet that starting in 1959, woodsmen would have to cut 12 cords of wood instead of eight to be entitled to unemployment insurance weekly benefits. That is an 80 per cent increase. Indeed, this is not, at least in my opinion, an improvement in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Another amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was the one brought about by Bill No. C-43 which increased employee and employer contributions. Again, that certainly was no way to help workers, since 75 per cent of the 100 odd million dollars we wanted to add to the unemployment insurance fund through contributions from employees and employers remain in the unemployment insurance fund. Therefore the instructions in form 13, as well as the new rules with regard to woodsmen and the rate increase, are certainly not changes in the unemployment insurance act that will be of help to our workers.
About those various laws, I cannot help referring to someone who is no longer in the house; I mean the former member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska, who stated here, last February, that his government had done nothing against unemployment, and had been content to introduce legislation which only contributed to deplete the unemployment insurance fund. As we may see in Le Devoir of February 20, 1960, the former member for Restigouche-Madawaska stated as follows:
I maintain, in all humility, that if we had only done half of what we had promised, there would be no unemployment now in the maritimes he said.

Unemployment Insurance
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the unemployment picture is right now in the county of Restigouche-Madawaska. But I wonder if the former member is making the same type of speeches there now as he used to when he was sitting in this house. I would be very happy to follow it up in the press.

I feel sure the hon. member does not even believe this attack he made on me and the rest of my party in this corner. If he does believe it, I am afraid that I have given the hon. gentleman far too much credit for intelligence. I feel that, in his search for a whipping boy, he has done a disservice to this house and to the country because he has done exactly what the communists are trying to do throughout the world today. They are trying to make us believe there is only one choice, either the chaos that we are debating here tonight or the regimentation that one finds under communist regimes. We can only choose between the two.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that we in the C.C.F. and new party repudiate this idea. We maintain that this problem can be cured while we maintain our political freedom. In order to cure these difficulties we must show more interest in coping with these problems than has been demonstrated by either the present Tory government or the Liberal governments of the past.
What is the situation with which we are faced here tonight? The parliamentary secretary says that the opposition finds itself in a dilemma. I should like to remind him that it is not the opposition that is going to have to answer to the Canadian people for the situation in which we find ourselves now. It is the government that is going to have to answer, and only the government.
What are the facts? They have been placed on the record today, and I think probably we could sum them up. When this government took office there was in the neighbourhood of $950 million in the unemployment insurance fund. Halfway through the government's term of office we find that contributions to the fund have been increased
