Unemployment Insurance by 30 per cent but still the size of the fund has shrunk to $185 million as of the latest count. The government can accuse the opposition of gloom and doom or this and that, but these are the cold, hard facts. We cannot get around them. During this government's term of office, in spite of this 30 per cent increase in the contributions into the fund, we find that the fund has shrunk from $950 million to $185 million.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext: What about the increased benefits?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DEPLETION OF FUND AND DENIAL OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I do not care what the increase is in benefits. These are the facts, and you cannot get around them.
In my opinion, these facts point out one thing which should be clear to each and every member. Surely, this is something hon. members must have realized some place along the way in their daily lives. So long as you pay more out of a fund than you pay into that fund you are eventually going to go broke. This is the very simple situation with which we are faced today. The parliamentary secretary listed three of the measures which the government had introduced, and then he was cut off. He said, however, that there were some 23 measures which this government had adopted during this session to aid employment and provide jobs. This statement still does not meet the point because if there were 23 measures or 63 or 6,300, the fact still remains that the unemployment insurance fund is almost bankrupt.
How did we get into this situation? The parliamentary secretary listed some of the reasons. The unemployment insurance fund was extended to take in new fields. Of course, he very carefully avoided mentioning the fact that no precaution was taken at that time to provide for these new fields. The extension of the benefits has gone over a longer period; they have been extended to 52 weeks. Again no provision was made at the time to put the fund on any kind of actuarial basis. Oh, no; the government could not wait for that. It was too good a vote catcher. They had to use it. At the time that amendment went through I can recall speaking in this house and warning the government then that if this was done and the proper precautions were not taken, in a very short period of time this fund would be completely depleted.
I can still recall the question asked by some hon. member on the government side who said, "Are you against extending unemployment insurance?"
Many other factors are involved. Not the least of these is the situation that has been brought about by the Liberals and then continued by the Tories which has permeated


our whole society on this matter of the unemployment insurance fund. There is no insurance principle about it at all. It is just a great big pork barrel. People see others drawing from it whom they feel are not qualified to do so and they say, "If they can get it, why can't I?". That is the situation that has developed across this country. But in spite of all these factors, including many smaller ones, we still cannot get around the basic problem.
This is a basic problem which the present government very stubbornly refused to recognize for a long time. Now they are very grudgingly starting to admit it. Nevertheless they are still stubbornly trying to refuse to act, and do anything about it. I refer to the fact that in the last three or four years we have had what used to be known in the old days as a depression. Of course, that is a bad word. We do not use it any more. Today it is a recession, a slow down. I do not know how many fancy names I have heard for it. Of course, the facts of the matter are that we have forgotten what the unemployment insurance fund was originally intended for. Back in the old days when the unemployment insurance fund was set up, it was for the purpose of tiding people over when they were temporarily laid off from a job which they had to go back to in the fall or in the spring. That was the purpose of the unemployment insurance fund when it started off. It was to tide people over when they were temporarily unemployed either through climatic conditions or the temporary shut-down of a plant or something of the kind.
But what do we do today with that fund that was designed for this purpose and was set up on this basis? As long as we stuck to this basis it was a very successful project. But no, the government did not do that. Now they are trying to cure this depression with this unemployment insurance fund. They take in people who were never even considered when this fund was set up on an actuarial basis. They extend it over a period of time which was never even considered when this fund was set up on a sensible basis.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that this unemployment insurance fund was never conceived of with the idea of curing a depression. It never can cure a depression and the reason we find ourselves in the present situation is that we have tried to use it for that purpose.
In trying to face this problem with which we are confronted and to do something about it I hope that the steps that this government and this house will take-and believe me the government will be obliged to take some steps and do so very shortly-will be sensible and reasonable steps and that they will not be caused by this hysteria that seems to be

sweeping across this country, that all of a sudden out of the woodwork or from some place where they have been hidden for the last 20 years all these bums are coming back again. It is strange that we did not hear about them in the 40's and 50's. Where were they then? We used to have a good many of them around in the 30's. I refer to bums, people who do not want to work. For 20 years we did not hear anything about them but today they are back with us again.
I do not care where you go, you find this thing building up. I feel that this idea has been very carefully planted. I feel it is another of the attempts of this government to find a whipping boy, as was done by the parliamentary secretary; to find somebody else to blame; to try to shrug off the responsibility that is theirs and theirs alone. They are the ones who are going to be obliged to do something about it. All we hear is about chiselers, people who do not want to work. We hear about married women who work only long enough to get their stamps and so on. We hear this every day on every side.
I want to say that I am quite concerned about this deliberate propaganda campaign. Certainly there are chiselers. There are chiselers in every walk of life. But thank goodness, the percentage is small. There always will be chiselers; I suppose there always were chiselers. But with this problem as it is today, to try to pass it off with a shrug of your shoulders and say that it is only bums and chiselers that are out of work is no solution to it, and this will just get us deeper and deeper into the mess in which we find ourselves at the present time. We hear about people who turn down jobs at $45 a week. It is said that those guys simply do not want to work or they would not turn down a job at $45 a week. Why do they turn these jobs down? Did we ever stop to think of the reasons why they might have done so? The previous answer may be true in some cases, but did we ever stop to realize that maybe these people are the victims of the society in which we live, that they are the victims of the hard-sell policy under which it is unpatriotic if you do not buy what you do not need with money you do not possess in order to impress people you do not like.
Do we stop to realize that almost every normal family in this country has payments to meet which amount to more than $45 a week? They are built-in payments. Back in the 30's if you had no job, at least you could go out to the edge of town, cut yourself a cord of wood and cook yourself a meal. However, you cannot do that today. If you do not pay your gas bill, your gas is cut off. If you do not pay your water bill, your water is cut off. If you do not pay your light bill, 90205-6-286
Unemployment Insurance your electricity is cut off. If you do not meet the payments on your stove or your refrigerator or on all the rest of your furniture, they come in, pick it up and take it out. If you are working for $45 a week, and that sum does not meet your payments, you are in trouble. But if you are unemployed and are on unemployment insurance when they come in, you can say, "I am sorry I cannot pay because I am unemployed"; and at least you can put off the inevitable. Maybe that is the reason why some in this country today are refusing jobs paying $45 a week or less.
I think these things should be taken into consideration. We must realize that our society has changed a great deal in the last 20 or 25 years and that we certainly cannot judge people's conduct today by the yardstick of 25 years ago. In order to get a proper look at the situation today and to try to come up with some sensible and reasonable answers to this problem we must look at these things in the light of today's conditions and then act accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, the unemployment insurance fund was started as an insurance for workers, to compensate them for periods of unemployment. It seems to me that in the administration of the act the government is departing a great deal from this insurance principle.

They have made it partly a relief fund. Money is taken from this fund to help people over difficult periods, when these people should be helped in other ways by the government. This has been bad administration of the fund, but it has been helpful to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). It has prevented his yearly deficits from being as high as they otherwise would be. The working people of Canada are, therefore, making contributions toward keeping people off relief rolls. In this way they have allowed the Minister of Finance to keep his bad budget showings during the last four years from being worse than they have been.
I saw an announcement some time ago that 44 claim investigators had been appointed to watch for fraudulent claims against the unemployment insurance fund, and I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) say on television that these people had been appointed and that any fraudulent claims made would result in prosecution. I have not yet heard of the results of any prosecutions which have taken place or how much money, if any, has been recovered, but I would say that the amount of money recovered is peanuts compared with the amount of money lost to the fund as a result of the fiscal policy of this government.
On May 3, the Minister of Finance reported that the amount of money to the credit of the fund as of March 31 was $185.4 million. This amount does not take into account the market value of $248.3 million worth of securities held in the portfolio. It means that the unemployment insurance fund is borrowing money against these bonds. It is hypothecating these bonds and borrowing money, so the real value of the unemployment insurance fund does not begin to equal the amount of bonds they hold. Back in 1959 we could not go to the bank and borrow money against these same bonds. The banks would not lend us money at that time. The market value of these bonds is less by $30.3 million in unpledged securities and by about $8.2 million in respect to pledged securities, being $38.5 million in all so that ait the present time the market value of the unemployment insurance fund account is about $38.5 million below the amount of $185.4 million which the minister told us on May 3 was in the account as of March 31 last.
The advisory committee reported that during 1958 and 1959 they had taken a loss through the sale of bonds to the extent of $27.7 million. When one adds this to the depreciation in the present holdings of $38.5 million, the result is a potential loss of $66.2 million through bad investments on the part 90205-6-286J
Unemployment Insurance of those charged with responsibility for the unemployment insurance account.
The Minister of Finance has told us that in discussing this question we are talking from hindsight. I know I criticized the conversion loan at the time. The portfolio of the fund was filled with bonds of the conversion loan. At that time interest rates went up by 50 per cent if the longer term conversion loans were bought. I said that interest rates would go up and that therefore bonds would go down in respect to all maturities at that time. I said this would happen in connection with the provinces and the municipalities.
This whole matter of extra debt and high interest rates is closely associated with the unemployment insurance fund or, indeed, with any other fund which holds government of Canada bonds. Debt has a lot to do with it. The extra interest on our aggregate debt at the end of this current fiscal year will be some $800 million since this government has come into power and not once have they paid the interest on the interest. When the government has to borrow, interest rates move upwards and at the same time the value of the securities held by the unemployment insurance commission goes down. In order to meet this debt the Minister of Finance has borrowed money and he has paid high interest rates. The rates have been getting higher and higher. This has been done at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada and at the expense of such funds as the unemployment insurance fund, the army benevolent fund and other similar funds under the control of this government. After all, these funds are trust funds. They belong to the working people and to the poor people of Canada and I do not think the fiscal policy of the government should be such as to put them in jeopardy. When the bond market goes down, interest rates go up and the value of holdings in the unemployment insurance fund decreases. I know that the Minister of Finance had this to say as reported on page 2267 of Hansard of February 21:
As long as the present government Is in office you may be sure it is not going to pay one cent more interest on the moneys it has to borrow than is strictly necessary.
The Minister of Finance has accused us of talking from hindsight. I say that he certainly has not shown much foresight and, indeed, he has not shown much hindsight, either, because when he has borrowed money he has paid higher interest rates and that has certainly shoved down the value of these bonds.
I see it is almost ten o'clock. I do not wish to take up the time of the house much longer but I do want to say that on July 1, 1957, at about the time this government came into

Unemployment Insurance power, there was $862 million in this fund. Today, with the securities at market value, it amounts to about $146 million. The fund is down by $716 million, and that is a lot of money.
